name: Albuterol (Salbutamol)

lead: Albuterol (salbutamol) is the common asthma rescue inhaler. Some recreational bodybuilders use it, along with other beta-2 agonists, to get leaner and keep muscle while cutting.

It activates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, raising cAMP, a signal also involved in fat breakdown and muscle effects. Oral use has been studied for muscle wasting and obesity, and human studies reported more lean mass and less fat mass. Its main studied purpose is relieving bronchospasm in asthma and COPD, and trials in healthy people seeking cosmetic changes were not found.

paras: In bodybuilding circles it is used during cutting phases, alongside a calorie deficit and training, with the aim of fat loss while keeping muscle. Most people know it as the inhaler form; the lean-mass studies used oral dosing. Users describe it as a cutting-phase add-on rather than a standalone fix.

Common effects are tremor, anxiety, headache, cramps, dry mouth and palpitations. Higher doses can cause fast heart rate, arrhythmia and low potassium. Asthma research has examined links between heavy beta-agonist use and asthma death. It is prescription-only in the US, UK and Canada, and beta-2 agonists are regulated in sport.

angle.text: Albuterol activates beta-2 receptors, which raises metabolic rate and is tied to lean-mass effects, so some bodybuilders use it for a leaner, more muscular look during cuts. Small studies of oral dosing reported more lean mass and less fat mass; its studied purpose is bronchospasm.

lead: Albuterol, known as salbutamol outside the US, is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist sold as Ventolin, ProAir and Proventil, among other brands. It is a first-line rescue bronchodilator for bronchospasm in asthma and COPD, and it is one of the most widely prescribed medicines in the United States [1][2][3].

Within physique-focused communities it is discussed as a beta-2 agonist in the same family as clenbuterol. Some lifters and bodybuilders use oral salbutamol in cutting phases because beta-2 receptor activation increases energy expenditure and lipolysis, which they hope will help them look leaner while keeping muscle [3][4]. Wikipedia reports that some recreational bodybuilders use it and that oral beta-2 agonists have been studied as anti-obesity and anti-muscle-wasting agents, with studies reporting more lean mass and less fat mass [3].

It was discovered in 1966 by a team led by David Jack at Allen & Hanburys, launched in the UK in 1969 as Ventolin and approved in the US in 1982 [3]. Published trials of salbutamol for cosmetic fat loss or muscle gain in healthy people were not found; the large body of trial work concerns asthma, COPD and related respiratory conditions [1][5][6].
infobox: Prescription-only (US, UK, Canada); on the WHO Essential Medicines List [3]

paras: Albuterol treats or prevents bronchospasm in asthma, including exercise-induced bronchospasm, and in COPD. It is the standard reliever in asthma guidelines, and the US label lists treatment or prevention of bronchospasm in people aged 4 years and older with reversible obstructive airway disease and prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm [1][2].

Other uses include lowering blood potassium in acute hyperkalemia, because it moves potassium into cells, and, historically, intravenous use to delay preterm labour, a role largely taken over by nifedipine [3][7]. Recent studies have also explored it in some congenital myasthenic syndromes and in spinal muscular atrophy [3][8].

Appearance-oriented use is mostly oral salbutamol tablets or syrup used by some bodybuilders during fat-loss phases, often discussed as a milder relative of clenbuterol. Forum posts describe its use alongside testosterone and other compounds during cuts, and some lifters who use a rescue inhaler for asthma describe it as helping them train harder [9][10]. Wikipedia states that some recreational bodybuilders use albuterol and does not describe off-label weight-loss use as widespread [3].
Posters on T Nation have cited the physiology as the rationale, noting that infusions of salbutamol and terbutaline in lean men modestly raised whole-body energy expenditure [11].

Wikipedia reports that salbutamol raises energy expenditure by about 10 to 15 percent at asthma doses and by about 25 percent at higher oral doses, and that studies of beta-2 agonists have shown increased lean mass, reduced fat mass and lipolysis [3]. These findings come from physiology and small clinical studies rather than from trials of cosmetic body recomposition in healthy people.

In respiratory medicine, albuterol rescue therapy is well established. Recent phase 3 trials compare albuterol alone with albuterol-budesonide combination rescue inhalers, reporting a lower risk of severe asthma exacerbation with the combination in moderate-to-severe asthma and in mild asthma [5][6][12].

Common effects are fine tremor, anxiety, headache, muscle cramps, dry mouth and palpitations. Less often, tachycardia, arrhythmia and flushing occur, and rarely myocardial ischemia. High or prolonged doses can cause low potassium (hypokalemia), especially with kidney failure or certain diuretics [3].

The US label warns of life-threatening paradoxical bronchospasm, cardiovascular effects, hypersensitivity reactions and hypokalemia, and says that needing more doses than usual can signal worsening asthma [2]. The most common adverse reactions in label trials were throat irritation, viral respiratory infections, upper respiratory inflammation, cough and musculoskeletal pain [2].

A 1992 Canadian case-control study examined whether regular use of beta-2 agonists was associated with death or near-death from asthma [13]. Cardiovascular effects are a recurring theme in discussion of oral beta-2 agonists in non-medical use.

A tertiary butyl group gives salbutamol selectivity for beta-2 receptors, which predominate on bronchial smooth muscle. Receptor activation raises intracellular cAMP and lowers calcium, relaxing the muscle, and it suppresses release of inflammatory mediators from mast cells, basophils and eosinophils [3]. Beta-2 receptors also exist in the heart (10 to 50 percent of cardiac beta receptors according to the label), which is why palpitations and tachycardia occur [2].

It is cleared by the kidneys, either directly or after conversion to a sulfate conjugate [3]. Salbutamol is sold as a racemic mixture (C13H21NO3). The R-enantiomer carries the bronchodilator activity, and levalbuterol is the single-enantiomer version; trials have compared it with racemic albuterol [3][14][15].

Salbutamol was developed at Allen & Hanburys in Ware, Hertfordshire, by a team led by David Jack, patented in Britain in 1966 and launched as Ventolin in 1969. It was approved in the US in 1982 [3]. In 2020 the FDA approved the first generic versions of albuterol inhalers, from Perrigo (ProAir HFA generic) and Cipla (Ventolin HFA generic) [3].
Salbutamol is the international non-proprietary name and albuterol the US name. In 2024 it was reported as the sixth most prescribed drug in the US, with more than 61 million prescriptions [3].

Anti-doping: inhaled salbutamol was banned at the 1972 Olympics but permitted by 1986; oral beta-2 agonists were not. WADA's 2011 list allowed inhaled use up to 1,600 micrograms over 24 hours, and Wikipedia states there was no evidence that inhaled salbutamol improves performance, though oral or intravenous use has been reported to [3]. A 2023 randomized trial reported that inhaled salbutamol may shorten time to exhaustion in some heavy endurance contexts [16].

Environmental discussion: Wikipedia notes that metered-dose inhalers were described as the largest source of carbon emissions from NHS medicines prescribing, and that dry powder inhalers are recommended as a lower-carbon option [3].

No studies found testing albuterol for cosmetic fat loss or muscle gain in healthy people. Related research includes studies of oral beta-2 agonists in obesity and muscle wasting that reported increased lean mass and reduced fat mass [3], and physiology studies showing raised energy expenditure [3][11].

Respiratory trials are extensive. The EPR-3 asthma guidelines position albuterol as a rescue medicine [1]. The 2022 MANDALA phase 3 trial and the 2025 BATURA trial tested as-needed albuterol-budesonide against albuterol alone [5][6], and the DENALI and TYREE trials examined the combination in mild-to-moderate asthma and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction [12][17]. A 2025 systematic review compared drugs for acute hyperkalaemia [7].
